articles.title: Miu Miu turns ‘real clothes’ into high fashion with sportswear style
articles.summary: Brand’s signature desire to subvert the ordinary brings blazers with track pants and crop tops under blazers to Paris fashion week. Speaking backstage at Miu Miu’s show on Sunday at Paris fashion week, Miuccia Prada said she had been thinking about “real clothes”.
body: The collection opened with a series of five neatly pleated checked skirts. The first was worn with an equally neat checked blazer but rather than a smart shoe, such as a pump or loafers, there were brightly coloured trainers. The second featured a crop top under the blazer, the trainers swapped for spiky high heels. The other looks ditched the blazer and clipped the tops so they sat just under the bust line.

Later came the type of track pants usually made for mooching around in; here they were paired with smart knitwear and tailored jackets. Gym knickers were given the same upgraded styling treatment, while sports bras were reimagined as sparkly tops, more party than pilates; some were worn solo, others over clingy jersey tops. Jeans, a collaboration with Wrangler to rework its vintage denim, hung low below hips. Instead of buttons, zips or even belts, there were fastenings that riffed on shoelaces.

Prada described the approach as “nonconformist dialogues exploring a form of friction and tension”. This method of clashing clothing genres and subverting the ordinary has turned Miu Miu into a near-billion-euro brand.

articles.title: Plot Twist! All the Books Guests Brought to the Valentino Show
articles.summary: Alessandro Michele asked attendees to his spring 2027 show—titled Antibiblioteca: Catalogue of the Unread—to bring a book that would be donated to a local library.
body: Fashion week is built around looking, but Valentino wanted its guests to do a little reading, too.

While a show invitation usually tells you where to be, when to arrive, and sometimes offers a cryptic clue as to what awaits on the runway (for Dior, it was a walnut. At Schiaparelli, a Kandi friendship bracelet); at Valentino’s spring 2027 show, Alessandro Michele asked guests to bring along a book. “New or from your own library,” read the small green card tucked inside the invitation. After the show, the collected volumes would be donated to local libraries.

I’m bringing a memoir by Claude Billen (Delay), published in 1973, dedicated to her dear friend Gabrielle Chanel. Claude is Coco Chanel’s last surviving friend, and it’s fascinating to read about the greatest fashion icon through the eyes of a friend.

This is where I studied literature and breathed in freedom, convinced that the future belongs to women. But we must never let our guard down: Natalia Aspesi’s words in this 1978 book are more relevant today than ever.

articles.title: Does the word ‘Dumbass’ flash up when your husband calls your phone? | Polly Hudson
articles.summary: From ‘Sharon London Sex’ to ‘Trashy Anne’, the names saved in our phones are tiny records of how relationships began. Why erase the evidence? At first glance, it’s such a simple, reasonable ask.
body: Personally, I’ve never got over noticing – on their reality show rather than while lunching – that Kim Kardashian has her mother saved as Kris Jenner instead of, say, Mom. It felt like an extremely revealing detail from the queen of the genre.

The Threads debate raised an interesting question, though: should your contact list be amended and updated, or preserved as a historical artefact? Perhaps the poster is underestimating the warm glow to the heart and soul he subconsciously receives whenever his wife’s name pops up and he’s transported back to the beginning of their unlikely love story. Living app-ily ever after is rare, after all.

Other replies echoed the notion that contacts provoke memories. “I’m coming up on the 10th anniversary of ‘Trashy Anne’ … who I got to know volunteering as bin collectors at a local festival,” said one. Another confided: “My best friend and I met through a mutual friend almost 15 years ago. I’m still ‘Ayannah (Gabby’s friend)’.” The comfort we get from a reminder of these origin stories may be more important than it seems.

articles.title: John Cooper Clarke looks back: ‘Getting older sucks – it’s marginally better than being dead’
articles.summary: The punk poet on his heroin years, dressing like Ronnie Wood, and achieving his boyhood ambition. Born in Salford in 1949, John Cooper Clarke is a poet and author. He cut his teeth in the clubs of Manchester before signing to Epic Records in 1978.
body: This is me dressed up as a cowboy with a hat and six-shooter. Not the full schmear with the chaps and all the rest, but the best I could do. I was crazy about westerns. Still am, actually. My uncle Dennis was the only camera-owning relative at the time, so he would have taken the photo in our apartment above a chemist’s shop in Salford, located on a busy traffic intersection.

My childhood is an ever-fading mystery to me, but somewhere around this time I know I got diagnosed with tuberculosis. Something serious like that takes you out of the world, but once I stopped coughing up arterial blood and scar tissue it wasn’t a problem. I stopped going to school, which was great, and not before I’d learned the rudiments of literacy. Really it happened at an opportune moment in that all that I had any energy to do was read.

articles.title: Björk Performs in the Mugler Collection She Inspired, the Same Day It Debuts in Paris
articles.summary: For his third collection at Mugler, Miguel Castro Freitas looked to nature, animal instinct, and the radical freedom of Björk. In tandem, the Icelandic artist wore a look straight from the runway to the DJ booth in Poland.
body: In perhaps the most fashionable scheduling conflict ever, Björk couldn’t attend the latest Mugler show, one that she inspired, no less. Alas, she was in Bielsko-Biała, Poland, for the opening weekend of her touring exhibition Björk: Ancestress, Sorrowful Soil & Nerve Bloom (remix), performing a special DJ set that closed the Wędrujący Festiwal. So the Icelandic artist did the most Björk thing possible: she wore a look from the collection the same day it debuted in Paris. Who needs front-row pomp when you have a Polish market full of ravers?

For this latest rendezvous, styled by longtime collaborator Edda Guðmundsdóttir, Björk became Mugler’s satellite record-spinning model in a purple butterfly-print second-skin top and black leather corseted high-waisted skirt. Above it hovered a magnificent bit of house history: a fringed feather headpiece from Manfred Thierry Mugler’s spring 1997 haute couture collection, Les Insectes. The result collapsed nearly 30 years of Mugler into one silhouette: part woman, part extraterrestrial.

articles.title: “Chloé Forever!” Chemena Kamali was the Toast of the Town During a Post-Show Dinner at Lapérouse
articles.summary: Chloé and creative director Chemena Kamali bookended the first day of October with a morning display of optimistic spring fashion and an evening of after-dark revelry with Claire Danes, Cynthia Erivo, Apple Martin, Natasha Lyonne, Maude Apatow, and more.
body: Just after 10 a.m., Cynthia Erivo was stopping traffic outside the show space on Avenue de l’Observatoire in a floor-sweeping bohemian black skirt and printed purple jacket—with her signature lengthy nails painted in coordinating hues. By nightfall, she’d traded her unique look for floaty teal plaid silk chiffon and oodles of sculptural hardware around her neck.

“People may not think I’m a ‘Chloé girl,’ but I am. I love—and buy—the clothes,” Erivo told Vogue during a post-show fête at Lapérouse. “Chloé can be for goths and edgy people, too. Plus I’m a geek, so I was busy looking at all the construction and the 1960s references to Chemena’s mum coming down the runway earlier.” A particular piece that piqued her attention was a juxtaposing “sexy and romantic” harness neckline gown in jet-black broderie anglaise—perhaps something you may see her step out in for her Hollywood Bowl concert later this month or a red carpet for the forthcoming Children of Blood and Bone.

articles.title: Behind the Scenes: Duran Lantink Defines His Vision for Ready-to-Wear at Jean Paul Gaultier
articles.summary: Vogue Business was a fly on the wall during creative director Lantink’s show fittings at the house HQ.
body: On the eve of his third ready-to-wear show for Jean Paul Gaultier, I met the house’s creative director, Duran Lantink, at the company’s headquarters on Rue Saint-Martin. Lantink works on fittings with London-based stylist Jodie Barnes.

I walk up the stairs and join him in a familiar space; this is where the couture shows take place. (Sunday’s ready-to-wear show is held at the Palais de Tokyo.) In the white-walled room with its high ceiling, there’s a model walking in low-rise jeans and a voluminous white top. “I like these jeans better than the ones before,” Barnes says. “Yes, and I like that the scorpion [the tattoo on the model’s belly] comes out,” Lantink adds.

Lantink was appointed creative director of the Puig-owned house in April 2025, assigned with leading both couture and ready-to-wear. Prior to his appointment, he helmed his eponymous label, founded in 2016, which joined the official fashion calendar in 2023. Barnes started working with the designer back then. “I love his raw talent. I think there’s a lot of freedom with him and the way he thinks, and I’m the same. Somehow, it comes together quite well,” she says.
